Originally Deep Web meant sites which can't be found via search engines, they aren't indexed by them. Dark Web was the TOR stuff.

Now the terms are often being used interchangeably and Deep Web is gradually becoming more and more of a synonym for Dark Web.
Dark web sites can only be accessed with a special browser. Deep web sites are often small sites that can't be found with a search engine.

Deep Web>Can't be found with a search engine
Dark Web>TOR, I2P etc

Deep web is all the data in back end databases that isn't directly available. For example, when you go to Amazon.com, you see some data on their front page. When you do a search, you see some more. All that data you don't see? That's the deep web. My personal account information that I can see, but you can't? That's the deep web. Same for Google and DuckDuckGo and Voat and .. well every site that has dynamic content. It's been estimated that 75% of all data on the Internet is in the Deep Web. All of the business data that companies keep on their employees, customers, etc. isn't usually considered part of the deep web, but it's still data we can't access.

The Dark Web is something altogether different. Using special networking software (e.g. TOR), you can get to web sites that you can't get to any other way. These sites usually contain information that is illegal in many places or the users want to hide for some other reason. It can also be used to hide your tracks if you want to contact someone (or cause mischief) without being able to be traced.

There's a Deep Web for the Dark Web, too. If you understood that sentence...you got it.
Deep web = searchable data on websites that aren't part of what a search engine can find. Dark web = purposefully hidden websites such as those only found on TOR

When you "observe" a ruler measuring a distance, what is really happening is a set of photons that strike the ruler and then consequently your eye, which understands how to process the sequence of photons from the million retinal cells, which lets you observe that something is x inches long. The key takeaway from this is that the photons have to interact with something (in this case, your cornea), for you to observe something.

Its simply the fact that in order to observe a particle, you have to interact with this, and this interaction is what causes the behavior to change.

So when you talk about entanglement, what happens is that the two wavefunctions of the two entangle particles are somehow correlated. We don't know exactly how they change, but what we do observe is that when we observe them both (i.e, interact with them somehow), the results are correlated in the sense that they are observed in an identical state.

Its akin to having a bag with 2 marbles, black and white. You can't see inside the bag, but you know that when you and your friend pull one, and you observe yours to be white, the other one will be black. However, you know why that is because you originally only put two in the bag. The difference with quantum entanglement, is that we are not sure of the underlying process of what causes 2 particles to be entangled. We know how to make entangled particles, but we don't have the current information to mathematically describe the exact process.
